section.title: Purity of the Camp
section.sectionRationale: Before Israel departs from Sinai, the camp itself must be kept ceremonially and morally pure: those defiled by disease or death are sent outside, wrongs against a neighbor must be confessed and repaid, and a suspected marital unfaithfulness is entrusted to God alone through a solemn ritual, together showing that the LORD who dwells in the midst of the camp demands purity in body, in restitution, and in the hidden places of the heart.
section.thesis: Because the LORD Himself dwells among His people, the camp must be kept clean from defilement, wrongs must be confessed and made right, and even secret unfaithfulness that no human court can prove is entrusted to God's own righteous judgment, showing that holiness reaches into what is hidden as well as what is seen.
section.frameNote: Four movements: sending the ceremonially unclean outside the camp; confession and restitution for wrongs done to another; the ritual law of jealousy for a wife suspected in secret; and the law's closing summary.

units.label: Sending out the unclean
units.note: so the camp where God dwells is not defiled

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Command the Israelites to send away from the camp anyone with a skin disease, anyone who has a bodily discharge, and anyone who is defiled by a dead body.
You must send away male and female alike; send them outside the camp so they will not defile their camp, where I dwell among them.”
So the Israelites did this, sending such people outside the camp. They did just as the LORD had instructed Moses.

units.label: Confession and restitution
units.note: repaying a wrong, plus a fifth

verses.text: And the LORD said to Moses,
“Tell the Israelites that when a man or woman acts {{unfaithful|unfaithfully}} against the LORD by committing any sin against another, that person is guilty
and must confess the sin he has committed. He must make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give all this to the one he has wronged.

But if the man has no relative to whom restitution can be made for the wrong, the restitution belongs to the LORD and must be given to the priest along with the ram of atonement, by which the atonement is made for him.
Every sacred contribution the Israelites bring to the priest shall belong to him.
Each man's sacred gifts are his own, but whatever he gives to the priest will belong to the priest.”

units.label: The law of jealousy: the ritual
units.note: God alone as judge of what cannot be proven

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and tell them that if any man's wife goes astray and is unfaithful to him
by sleeping with another man, and it is concealed from her husband and her impurity is undetected, since there is no witness against her and she was not caught in the act,

and if a feeling of {{jealousy|jealousy}} comes over her husband and he suspects his wife who has defiled herself, or if a feeling of jealousy comes over him and he suspects her even though she has not defiled herself,

then he is to bring his wife to the priest. 
He must also bring for her an offering of a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. He is not to pour oil over it or put frankincense on it, because it is a grain offering for jealousy, an offering of memorial as a reminder of iniquity.
The priest is to bring the wife forward and have her stand before the LORD.
Then he is to take some holy water in a clay jar and put some of the dust from the tabernacle floor into the water.

After the priest has the woman stand before the LORD, he is to let down her hair and place in her hands the grain offering of memorial, which is the grain offering for jealousy. The priest is to hold the bitter water that brings a curse.

And he is to put the woman under oath and say to her, ‘If no other man has slept with you and you have not gone astray and become defiled while under your husband's authority, may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse.
But if you have gone astray while under your husband's authority and have defiled yourself and lain carnally with a man other than your husband',
and the priest shall have the woman swear under the oath of the curse, ‘then may the LORD make you an attested curse among your people by making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell.

May this water that brings a curse enter your stomach and cause your belly to swell and your thigh to shrivel.’ 
Then the woman is to say, ‘Amen, Amen.’
And the priest shall write these curses on a scroll and wash them off into the bitter water.
He is to have the woman drink the bitter water that brings a curse, and it will enter her and cause her bitter suffering.
The priest shall take from her hand the grain offering for jealousy, wave it before the LORD, and bring it to the altar.
Then the priest is to take a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burn it on the altar; after that he is to have the woman drink the water.

When he has made her drink the water, if she has defiled herself and been unfaithful to her husband, then the water that brings a curse will enter her and cause bitter suffering; her belly will swell, her thigh will shrivel, and she will become accursed among her people.
But if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children.
This is the law of jealousy when a wife goes astray and defiles herself while under her husband's authority,
or when a feeling of jealousy comes over a husband and he suspects his wife. He is to have the woman stand before the LORD, and the priest is to apply to her this entire law.
The husband will be free from guilt, but the woman shall bear her iniquity.”

unfaithful.gloss: Unfaithfulness, trespass, or treachery. Elsewhere in Scripture this word describes covenant betrayal against the LORD Himself, so a wrong done against another person is here treated as unfaithfulness against God, not merely a private matter between neighbors.

jealousy.gloss: Jealousy or zeal, a strong emotion that can be destructive suspicion or righteous zeal depending on context. Here it describes a husband's suspicion, which the law refuses to let stand as proof; only God's own verdict, not human accusation, settles the matter.

basic.context: As Israel prepares to break camp from Sinai, God gives instructions to guard the purity of the community He dwells among: the ceremonially unclean must be sent outside the camp, wrongs against another person must be confessed and repaid with interest, and a wife secretly suspected of unfaithfulness undergoes a solemn ritual that leaves the verdict entirely in God's hands.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a specific set of case laws for ancient Israel's camp life and legal system, not a repeatable ceremony for today. Its most difficult section, the bitter water ordeal, must be read carefully: it protected an accused woman from vigilante justice or an accuser's mere assumption, since only God, not a human court or the husband himself, determined guilt.
basic.originalLanguages: The law addresses a husband's feeling of qinah, jealousy, and a wife's possible maal, unfaithfulness or trespass, framing marital betrayal as ultimately a sin against God Himself, not merely against a spouse, since the sanctuary dust and holy water at the center of the ritual involve the LORD directly as judge.
basic.typology: The sending of the unclean outside the camp anticipates the greater cleansing accomplished by Christ, who bore uncleanness outside the camp at the cross, Hebrews 13:12-13, so that His people could be brought fully into God's presence rather than kept at a distance.
basic.christ: Where this law required confession and repayment with an added fifth for wrongs done, and left hidden unfaithfulness to God's own judgment, Christ both makes atonement for sin and searches the hidden heart, John 2:24-25, fulfilling the pattern of a God who deals honestly with both open guilt and secret betrayal.
basic.god: God cares about the purity of the community He dwells among, in matters of health, of interpersonal wrong, and of hidden marital faithfulness. He is not only just in dealing with obvious sin but also entrusts what cannot be proven by human courts entirely to His own righteous knowledge and judgment.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 13:12-13 speaks of Jesus suffering outside the camp to sanctify His people. Leviticus 6:1-7 parallels the restitution plus a fifth required here for wrongs against a neighbor. 1 Corinthians 4:5 says the Lord will bring hidden things to light, echoing the jealousy law's confidence in God's just verdict.
basic.oneStory: From the earliest days of the wilderness camp, God cares about purity that is physical, relational, and hidden, providing means of cleansing, restitution, and just verdict even where human courts cannot see. That concern for holiness in every dimension of life finds its answer in Christ, who cleanses what is unclean and judges what is hidden.

context.literary:
Numbers 5 is built from three speeches, each opened by the same formula, 'the LORD said to Moses,' verses 1, 5 and 11. The three laws look unrelated at first, a public health order, a rule about restitution, and a marital ordeal, but they are arranged on a line that runs from the visible to the invisible. A skin disease or a discharge can be seen by anyone. A wrong against a neighbour is known at least to the one who did it and the one who suffered it. The hidden adultery of verse 13 is known to no human witness at all. The chapter walks the reader inward, from the body to the conscience to the secret places of a marriage, and insists that the holiness of the camp reaches all three.

A single verb stitches the second and third laws together. The man or woman who 'acts unfaithfully against the LORD' in verse 6 and the wife who 'is unfaithful to him' in verse 12 are described with the same Hebrew word. The neighbour who is cheated and the husband who is betrayed are both wronged in a way that God counts as a breach against Himself.

The first unit closes with an obedience report, verse 4, 'They did just as the LORD had instructed Moses,' a refrain that runs through these opening chapters. The third unit closes with a legal summary, 'This is the law of jealousy,' verses 29 to 31, in the style of the summaries that end the purity laws of Leviticus. Its own narration is looping rather than linear: the woman is made to stand before the LORD in verse 16 and again in verse 18, and the drinking is mentioned in verse 24 before the offering is burned and the drinking is described again in verses 26 and 27. The procedure is told once as an outline and then filled in.

Placed after the census and the arrangement of the tribes around the tabernacle in chapters 1 to 4, and before the dedication gifts of chapter 7, this chapter turns from the shape of the camp to its condition. A camp can be perfectly ordered on the outside and still defiled within.
context.historical:
The first hearers were a people camped in formation around a portable sanctuary, Numbers 2:2, with the Levites pitched closest to it 'so that no wrath will fall on the congregation,' Numbers 1:53. The three conditions named in verse 2 correspond to three blocks of purity law. Skin disease is treated in Leviticus 13 and 14, where the sufferer must 'live alone in a place outside the camp,' Leviticus 13:46. Bodily discharges are the subject of Leviticus 15, which ends with the warning that Israel must be kept from uncleanness 'so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them,' Leviticus 15:31. Corpse impurity is handled fully in Numbers 19. None of these conditions is called sin. They are states of ritual uncleanness, bound up with disease and death, that cannot share space with the living God.

The restitution law assumes the case already laid down in Leviticus 6:1-7, where a man who has defrauded his neighbour and sworn falsely must repay in full, add a fifth and bring a ram. Numbers adds two things. It makes confession explicit, and it answers a practical question: what happens if the wronged person has died and has no kinsman to receive the payment? Then it goes to the priest, verse 8.

Trial by ordeal was well known in the ancient Near East. The Code of Hammurabi, for example, sent a wife accused by others, but not caught, into the river; if she survived she was cleared. Israel's rite differs at the point that matters most. Water mixed with a little dust is harmless. Nothing in the procedure itself could hurt an innocent woman, so a guilty verdict required God to act. The ordeal in the river presumed guilt unless the gods intervened; this rite presumed innocence unless the LORD intervened.

This is the only ordeal in the law of Moses. The Mishnah, in the tractate named after the wayward wife, preserves a tradition that the practice was discontinued in the first century.
context.canonical:
The purity of the camp is a theme Numbers returns to at once. Miriam is shut outside the camp with a skin disease, and the whole people wait until she is brought back in, Numbers 12:14-15. The soldiers returning from Midian stay outside the camp seven days, Numbers 31:19. Deuteronomy gives the reason in a sentence: 'the LORD your God walks throughout your camp,' so 'your camp must be holy,' Deuteronomy 23:14. King Uzziah, who was 'unfaithful to the LORD his God' in the temple, lived out his days a leper, 'cut off from the house of the LORD,' 2 Chronicles 26:16 and 26:21, joining the two ideas of this chapter in one life.

The law of jealousy becomes a language for the covenant. The LORD calls Himself jealous, Exodus 20:5, and even says His name is Jealous, Exodus 34:14. The prophets picture Israel as a wife gone astray: Hosea's marriage, Jeremiah's certificate of divorce for faithless Israel, Jeremiah 3:8, and Ezekiel's sentence on Jerusalem as an adulterous wife, bringing 'the wrath of your bloodshed and jealousy,' Ezekiel 16:38. Yet Hosea also hears God promise, 'I will betroth you to Me forever,' Hosea 2:19.

In the New Testament the three laws resurface in the ministry of Jesus. He touches a leper, a woman with a twelve year flow of blood touches Him, and He touches the coffin of a widow's son, Mark 1:41, Mark 5:27 and Luke 7:14, and in each case the cleanness flows outward from Him. Zacchaeus goes beyond the law's added fifth, Luke 19:8. Jesus makes reconciliation with a brother the condition of offering a gift, Matthew 5:23-24. When a woman caught in adultery is dragged before Him, John 8:3-11, the case is the reverse of this chapter's, a public charge rather than a hidden suspicion, and He turns the scrutiny back on the accusers. Paul speaks of 'a godly jealousy' for the church he has promised to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and Hebrews calls believers to go to Jesus 'outside the camp,' Hebrews 13:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to grasp that the presence of God in the middle of the camp changed everything about ordinary life. The reason given in verse 3 governs the whole chapter: 'their camp, where I dwell among them.' Uncleanness is not only a private misfortune; it is incompatible with the dwelling of the Holy One.

He also meant them to learn that sin against a neighbour is never merely horizontal. By calling a wrong against another person unfaithfulness 'against the LORD,' verse 6, he taught that the one who cheats a neighbour has trespassed on God's property, since every Israelite belongs to Him. Repair has to run in both directions: confession and payment to the neighbour, atonement with God.

Finally, he wanted a people prone to suspicion to know that there is a limit to what human beings may do with what they cannot prove. A husband could not act on his feelings, and a community could not act on rumour. The case had to be brought to the LORD, who alone knows what happened in secret, and the chapter's last word, verse 31, clears the husband who brought the case honestly while leaving the guilty, if she is guilty, to carry her own iniquity before God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is law, so it prescribes, but it prescribes for a specific covenant order: a camp gathered around a tabernacle, with priests, holy water and an altar. Those structures have been fulfilled in Christ, and the church neither sends the sick outside its gatherings nor administers the bitter water. The Jewish community itself ceased the ordeal long ago.

What carries forward is the moral logic. Wrongs against people are wrongs against God and require confession and real repair, not only an apology; Jesus says the same, Matthew 5:23-24. Holiness is expected in hidden things as much as in public ones. And suspicion must never be turned into a verdict without proof. The church's discipline requires witnesses, Matthew 18:16, and whatever cannot be proven is left to the Lord who 'will bring to light what is hidden in darkness,' 1 Corinthians 4:5.

debates.question: Was the law of jealousy, verses 11 to 31, oppressive to women, or protective?

views.label: A protective safeguard for the accused woman
views.case: The law takes the matter out of the husband's hands and away from the crowd. He cannot punish her himself; he must bring an offering and submit his suspicion to the priest and to God. The rite uses harmless materials, so an innocent woman had nothing to fear from the water, and verse 28 promises that she will be unaffected and able to conceive. Verse 14 even contemplates that the husband's suspicion may be groundless. Compared with ordeals elsewhere that presumed guilt, this presumes innocence.

views.label: A law shaped by its patriarchal setting
views.case: Others point out that the procedure is one sided. There is no matching rite for a wife who suspects her husband, the woman is put through a public humiliation with her hair unbound, and verse 31 clears the husband of guilt whatever the outcome. The law restrains a husband's jealousy but also gives it a formal outlet.

debates.bearing: Both observations are true. The law works within the marriage customs of its world while pushing hard against their worst abuses, and its deepest claim is theological: only God may convict in secret matters. The later prophets turn the picture around, making Israel the unfaithful wife and the LORD the wronged husband who nonetheless promises to betroth her again, Hosea 2:19-20.

debates.question: What does the curse of the swelling belly and shrivelling thigh describe, verses 21, 22 and 27?

views.label: Miscarriage of a pregnancy conceived in adultery
views.case: Some read the case as one in which the woman is already pregnant and the husband suspects the child is not his. The swelling and shrivelling would then describe the loss of the pregnancy, and several modern translations render the phrase along those lines.

views.label: Barrenness or a disease of the reproductive organs
views.case: Others note that the reward of innocence in verse 28 is being 'able to conceive children,' which suggests the curse is the opposite, lasting infertility, perhaps through some physical disorder. The thigh is often used in Hebrew as a modest way of referring to the reproductive body.

debates.bearing: The exact condition cannot be fixed with certainty, and the text is content to be reticent. What is clear is that the sentence strikes the sphere of the sin, and that the woman becomes 'an attested curse among her people,' verse 21, a public sign that God sees what men cannot.

study.originalLanguages:
The unclean person of verse 2 is literally 'unclean for a nephesh.' Nephesh, the familiar word for soul or living being, is used here and in Numbers 6:6 and Leviticus 21:1 for a dead person. The word that names life names its absence too, as if to say that a corpse is a life that has departed. The adjective tame, unclean, is the key term of the Levitical purity laws; it describes a state, not a moral fault, and the cure is washing and waiting, not repentance.

God's reason in verse 3, 'where I dwell among them,' uses the participle of shakan, to dwell, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle. The verb is present tense in force: He is dwelling there now. Numbers 35:34 repeats the thought for the land, 'For I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.'

In verses 6 to 8 the word asham does triple duty. The person 'is guilty,' verse 6; he must make 'restitution,' verse 7; and the restitution goes to the LORD if there is no relative, verse 8. All three render the same root, the one that also names the guilt offering of Leviticus 5 and 6. Guilt, in this way of speaking, is a debt that must be paid, and the payment carries the name of the debt. Isaiah uses the same word when he says the Servant's soul is made 'a guilt offering,' Isaiah 53:10. The verb 'confess' in verse 7 is a reflexive form of yadah, to acknowledge or praise; it is the verb of Leviticus 5:5 and of the national confession of Leviticus 26:40. The 'relative' of verse 8 is the goel, the kinsman redeemer who recovers a family's losses, Leviticus 25:25 and Ruth 3:12. If no goel exists, God Himself stands in that place and receives what is owed.

The wife who 'goes astray' in verse 12 is described with satah, to turn aside, the verb Proverbs uses of the young man warned 'do not stray into her paths,' Proverbs 7:25. Later Jewish tradition named the whole rite after this word. The husband's feeling in verse 14 is a 'spirit of jealousy,' ruach qinah; the grain offering of verse 15 is 'an offering of memorial as a reminder of iniquity,' two words from the root zakar, to remember. The offering does not accuse her; it brings the matter to God's remembrance and leaves it with Him. Like the poor person's sin offering of Leviticus 5:11, it has no oil and no frankincense, the elements of joy and fragrance withheld.

The priest 'lets down her hair,' verse 18, with the verb para, used of the diseased person who must 'let his hair hang loose,' Leviticus 13:45, and of the mourning Aaron was forbidden, Leviticus 10:6. The gesture places her, for the moment, in the posture of the unclean and the grieving. 'The bitter water that brings a curse' is a sound play in Hebrew, mey hammarim hameararim, bitter and cursing echoing each other. Verse 23 says the priest writes the curses on a scroll and 'washes them off,' with machah, the verb Moses uses when he asks to be blotted out of God's book, Exodus 32:32. The words of the oath are literally dissolved into what she drinks. Her double 'Amen, Amen,' verse 22, is the same solemn assent the people give to the curses of Deuteronomy 27:15 and to Ezra's blessing, Nehemiah 8:6. By it she places herself under God's judgment of her own accord.

Finally, the closing verdict in verse 31 contrasts two states: the husband 'will be free from guilt,' from naqah, to be clean or acquitted, while the woman 'shall bear her iniquity,' the idiom nasa avon, to carry the weight of one's own sin before God.

typology.type: The unclean sent outside the camp, Numbers 5:2-4
typology.fulfillment: The camp could stay holy only by removing the unclean; holiness protected itself by exclusion. Jesus reverses the direction. He touches the leper and the dead, and instead of being defiled He makes clean, Mark 1:41-42 and Luke 7:14. Then He Himself goes outside, suffering 'outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12, taking the place of the excluded so that the excluded can be brought in. The type falls short because exclusion could protect the camp but never heal the sufferer, whereas Christ both heals and bears the reproach, and calls His people to go to Him 'outside the camp,' Hebrews 13:13.

typology.type: Restitution with the ram of atonement, Numbers 5:7-8
typology.fulfillment: The guilty person repays the neighbour with a fifth added and brings a ram of atonement to God. The two debts are distinct and both must be met. Isaiah 53:10 uses the very word for this payment, asham, of the Servant whose soul is made a guilt offering, so that in Christ the debt owed to God is paid in full by another. The type is exceeded in two ways: the ram covered one wrong, while Christ's offering covers all, and the repayment to the neighbour now springs from grace rather than preceding it, as when Zacchaeus, having received Jesus, gives fourfold, Luke 19:8.

typology.type: The bitter water that brings a curse, Numbers 5:18-27
typology.fulfillment: The accused drank a cup that would bring the curse only if she was guilty. The prophets speak of the cup of God's wrath that unfaithful Jerusalem must drink, Isaiah 51:17. In Gethsemane Jesus prays, 'let this cup pass from Me,' and then accepts it, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' Matthew 26:39 and John 18:11. The New Testament does not draw the line to Numbers 5 explicitly, so this is a fair echo rather than a declared type. The contrast is the point: the innocent One drinks the cup of the curse, and the guilty go free, Galatians 3:13.

typology.type: The husband's jealousy over a wife who may have gone astray, Numbers 5:14
typology.fulfillment: The law protects the bond of marriage from secret betrayal. Scripture uses that bond for God and His people, and Paul feels 'a godly jealousy' for a church he has promised 'to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ,' 2 Corinthians 11:2. Christ does not wait to test His bride; He gives Himself up for her 'to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,' so that she may stand 'without stain,' Ephesians 5:25-27. Where the ritual could only expose guilt, the Bridegroom removes it.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by contrast, and the contrast begins with touch. The law's answer to uncleanness was separation, because uncleanness was contagious and holiness had to be guarded. In the Gospels the contagion runs the other way. 'Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man,' Mark 1:41, and the leper was cleansed. A woman whose flow of blood would have kept her outside the camp touches His cloak and is healed, Mark 5:25-29. He touches a coffin, Luke 7:14, and the dead man sits up. The three conditions of Numbers 5:2, skin disease, discharge and death, all meet Jesus, and none of them defiles Him. He is the dwelling of God among people, John 1:14, and His holiness is not fragile but conquering.

It leads to Christ by the way of atonement. The man who wronged his neighbour needed both to repay the neighbour and to be reconciled to God with 'the ram of atonement,' verse 8. The Servant of Isaiah 53:10 is made an asham, the same word the chapter uses for restitution. On the cross the debt that no sinner could pay to God is paid, and the church then learns to repair what it can toward others, as Zacchaeus does, Luke 19:8, and as Jesus commands, Matthew 5:23-24.

It leads to Christ as the searcher of hearts. The law of jealousy exists because some things cannot be proven by any witness. John says Jesus 'knew what was in man,' John 2:25, and Paul says that when the Lord comes 'He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of men's hearts,' 1 Corinthians 4:5. The same Lord who sees in secret will one day judge in the open.

It leads to Christ as the one who drinks the cup. The accused woman lifted a vessel of water that carried the written curse. In the garden Jesus lifted a cup He did not deserve and drank it for those who did, Matthew 26:39, becoming 'a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. Her 'Amen, Amen' put her under the curse if she were guilty; His obedience removed the curse from the guilty.

Finally it leads to Christ as the faithful Bridegroom. The chapter imagines a marriage broken in secret. The gospel describes a Husband who knows all of His bride's unfaithfulness and still loves her and gives Himself for her, Ephesians 5:25-27. A caution is fitting: the dust, the clay jar and the hair are not coded prophecies. The links rest on the chapter's own concerns, uncleanness, guilt, hidden sin and a curse, which the New Testament shows Christ bearing and overcoming.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He dwells. Verse 3 does not say the camp must be pure because rules are rules; it says 'I dwell among them.' His holiness is not a remote principle but a presence, and presence changes the meaning of every tent pitched around the tabernacle. The same God later says, 'Do not defile the land where you live and where I dwell,' Numbers 35:34. Purity is simply what it means to live next door to the Holy One.

He is the owner and guardian of every person. A wrong against a neighbour is 'unfaithfully against the LORD,' verse 6. God treats harm to His image bearers as harm to Himself, and when the wronged man has no kinsman left, God Himself receives the restitution, verse 8. No debt of justice simply vanishes because the victim has died. God is the kinsman of those who have none.

He sees in secret. The whole third law rests on a case in which 'there is no witness against her,' verse 13. Human justice has run out, and God's has not. Psalm 139 prays, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart,' Psalm 139:23, and this chapter shows why that prayer is both frightening and safe. It is frightening to the guilty, because the hidden thing will be found. It is safe for the innocent, because the God who knows the truth will clear them, verse 28, even when a husband's suspicion and a community's whispers have not.

He is jealous, and His jealousy is holy. The word used of the husband's feeling is the word God uses of Himself, Exodus 34:14. It is not insecurity but the rightful claim of covenant love that will not share the beloved with another. That is why the prophets could picture idolatry as adultery, and why God's jealousy is always bound to His purpose to win His people back, Hosea 2:19-20.

He holds justice and mercy together. The chapter includes exclusion and a curse, and yet each law also provides a way through: the unclean may be cleansed and return, the guilty may confess and be atoned for, the innocent may be vindicated. God's holiness makes demands, but it also makes provision.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to bring God what we cannot resolve ourselves: suspicions we cannot prove, wrongs we cannot fully repay, uncleanness we cannot wash away. Proverbs 28:13 gives the pattern, 'whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy,' and 1 John 1:9 fills it out: He is 'faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us.'

crossReferences.note: The fullest description of the skin disease that Numbers 5:2 sends outside. The sufferer must let his hair hang loose, cry 'Unclean, unclean!' and live alone outside the camp. The same loosening of the hair is imposed on the accused wife in Numbers 5:18, placing her for a time in the posture of the excluded.

The theological reason behind the first law of Numbers 5. Israel must be kept separate from uncleanness 'so that they do not die by defiling My tabernacle, which is among them.' Numbers 5:3 gives the same reason in terms of God's dwelling in the camp.

The base law that Numbers 5:5-10 assumes. A man who defrauds his neighbour must restore in full, add a fifth and bring a ram as a guilt offering. Numbers adds explicit confession and provides for the case where the injured party has no kinsman left to receive the payment.

States the principle behind the whole chapter in a single sentence: the LORD walks throughout the camp, so the camp must be holy, lest He see anything unclean and turn away. Holiness is required because the presence is real.

Jesus puts the order of Numbers 5:6-8 into the life of discipleship. A worshipper who remembers that his brother has something against him must leave his gift at the altar and be reconciled first. Repair toward the neighbour belongs to right worship of God.

Zacchaeus, having welcomed Jesus, promises to repay anyone he has cheated fourfold, the higher rate of Exodus 22:1 rather than the added fifth of Numbers 5:7. Restitution here flows from grace received, not as a condition of receiving it.

A leper, one of those Numbers 5:2 sent from the camp, kneels before Jesus. Moved with compassion, Jesus touches him and he is cleansed. The holiness of God in Christ does not retreat from uncleanness but overcomes it.

The bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, and Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify His people. The place of the excluded in Numbers 5 becomes the place of salvation, and believers are called to go to Him there, bearing His disgrace.

After the long indictment of Israel as an unfaithful wife, the LORD promises to betroth her to Himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion and faithfulness. The jealous husband of Numbers 5 becomes, in God's case, the husband who restores.

Paul is 'jealous for you with a godly jealousy,' because he has promised the church to one husband, Christ. The feeling that Numbers 5:14 regulates in a human marriage is here the proper zeal of an apostle for the faithfulness of Christ's bride.

Paul tells the church to judge nothing before the appointed time, because the Lord will bring to light what is hidden and expose the motives of hearts. This is the conviction behind the jealousy law: secret matters belong to God's judgment, not to human suspicion.

In the new Jerusalem nothing unclean will ever enter, but only those written in the Lamb's book of life. The purity that Numbers 5 guarded by sending the unclean out is finally achieved by making God's people clean and bringing them in.

study.oneStory:
In Eden God walked with humanity in the garden, and after the fall the man and woman were sent out, Genesis 3:23-24. From then on the question of Scripture is how a holy God can dwell among an unclean people. At Sinai the answer begins to take shape. God pitches His tent in the middle of Israel's camp, and chapters like this one explain what that means: disease and death must be kept at a distance, wrongs must be confessed and repaid, and even secret sin is answerable to Him. Numbers 5 is Eden's exclusion in miniature, repeated daily in the life of a camp, with the difference that now there are ways back: washing, waiting, confession and atonement.

The rest of Israel's story shows how hard it was to keep that camp clean. The people grumble, rebel and die in the wilderness. In the land they bring idolatry into the very temple, and the prophets describe them as the wife of Numbers 5, gone astray in secret and then openly. God's jealousy leads to exile, Jeremiah 3:8, yet His promise holds, Hosea 2:19-20.

The story turns in Christ. God's dwelling takes flesh, John 1:14, and walks among the unclean, touching lepers, the bleeding and the dead without being defiled. He goes outside the camp to suffer, Hebrews 13:12, becomes the guilt offering that settles the debt owed to God, Isaiah 53:10, and drinks the cup of the curse. The Spirit then makes the church itself God's temple, 2 Corinthians 6:16, and the holiness once required of a camp is now required of a people who are called to confession, restitution and faithfulness in secret.

The story ends where the camp pointed. In the new Jerusalem God dwells with His people, 'nothing unclean will ever enter it,' Revelation 21:27, and there is no more death, Revelation 21:4. No one is sent outside for disease or death, because neither exists. No hidden unfaithfulness remains to be tested, because the bride has been made pure. What Numbers 5 could only protect for a season, God will make permanent, a holy people living with a holy God, with nothing left to separate them.

quiz.q: Who was to be sent outside the camp according to the opening instructions of this chapter?

options.text: Anyone with a skin disease, anyone with a bodily discharge, and anyone defiled by contact with a dead body.
options.note: Verse 2 lists these three conditions exactly.

options.text: Only foreigners living among Israel.
options.note: The instruction applies to Israelites, male and female alike, verse 3, not specifically foreigners.

options.text: Anyone who disagreed with Moses.
options.note: This is not mentioned anywhere in the chapter.

options.text: No one; the camp had no such requirement.
options.note: Verses 2 to 4 give this requirement explicitly.

quiz.q: What did the law require of someone who sinned against another person and was found guilty?

options.text: Full confession and full restitution of the wrong, plus an additional fifth of its value.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 state this requirement exactly.

options.text: Only a verbal apology, without any repayment.
options.note: The text explicitly requires repayment, not merely an apology.

options.text: Permanent exile from the camp.
options.note: This is not the consequence stated for this offense.

options.text: No requirement is given.
options.note: Verses 6 to 7 state the requirement plainly.

quiz.q: What was the priest to do if a husband suspected his wife of unfaithfulness but had no witness or proof?

options.text: Bring her before the LORD and follow the prescribed grain offering and water ritual, letting God reveal the truth.
options.note: Verses 12 to 28 describe this entire procedure.

options.text: Immediately have her stoned on the husband's word alone.
options.note: The text requires a whole process before the LORD, not immediate punishment on accusation.

options.text: Simply believe the husband's accusation without any further process.
options.note: An entire ritual process is prescribed instead of accepting the accusation alone.

options.text: The text gives no procedure for this situation.
options.note: Verses 12 to 28 describe the procedure in detail.

quiz.q: What happened to a woman who underwent the ritual and was innocent?

options.text: She was unaffected by the water and would be able to conceive children.
options.note: Verse 28 states this outcome for an innocent woman.

options.text: She was still exiled from the camp regardless of her innocence.
options.note: This contradicts the explicit vindication described in verse 28.

options.text: She had to pay a fine to her husband even if found innocent.
options.note: No such fine is mentioned in the text.

options.text: The text does not describe the outcome for an innocent woman.
options.note: Verse 28 describes this outcome directly.

quiz.q: According to the chapter's closing summary, who bears the guilt if the ritual reveals the wife was truly unfaithful?

options.text: The husband is free from guilt in bringing the matter before the LORD, but the guilty wife bears her own iniquity.
options.note: Verses 30 to 31 state this division of responsibility exactly.

options.text: The priest bears the guilt for administering the ritual, regardless of outcome.
options.note: No such statement about the priest's guilt appears in the text.

options.text: Guilt is shared equally between husband and wife regardless of the outcome.
options.note: Verse 31 assigns guilt specifically, not equally regardless of outcome.

options.text: The text assigns no responsibility for guilt at all.
options.note: Verse 31 addresses this directly.

questions: God required that even the ceremonially unclean be sent outside the camp so His dwelling among His people would not be defiled. What areas of your life do you keep too close to what you know displeases God?
Confession of sin was to be followed by real restitution, not just words. Is there a wrong you have named to God but never actually made right with the person you wronged?

The jealousy law entrusted what could not be proven to God's own judgment rather than human suspicion. Where are you carrying suspicion or an unresolved accusation that you need to hand over to God rather than try to resolve on your own?

An innocent woman under this law was explicitly vindicated, not merely tolerated. How does knowing God actively vindicates the innocent shape how you wait for justice in situations where you have been wrongly accused?

This whole chapter assumes that God's presence in the camp makes purity, honesty, and faithfulness matter in every corner of life, public and private. What hidden area of your life would look different if you truly believed God was as present there as anywhere else?

translationNotes.note: Acts unfaithfully against the LORD by committing any sin against another shows the Hebrew maal treats wrongs against a neighbor as simultaneously an offense against God.

The bitter water that brings a curse combines holy water with dust from the tabernacle floor and ink washed from a written curse, making the ritual itself, not human accusation, the instrument that would reveal guilt or innocence.
The woman shall bear her iniquity clarifies that the ritual's outcome, not the husband's initial suspicion, determines guilt; an innocent woman bears nothing.
